source_text: Qui autem sentiunt in processu, non semper a necessario, sed multa a possibili capiunt. Hoc in cunctis licet videre corporibus, sed longior disputatio nascitur; pauca tamen demus exempla. Natura corporum est, ut coagmentatione concrescant, divisione solvantur; capacia ergo sunt vulneris, quae patiuntur interitum. Ut ergo possint vulnerari, a necessario habent; ut vulnerentur autem, a possibili. Ita a necessario est possibilitatis natura, cum non sit necessarius possibilitatis effectus. Verbi gratia, equus, bos, et similes animantes vulnerabilem habent naturam, et ideo incommodi capacia a necessario sunt; ut autem vulnerentur, non semper necessarium est. Si enim per diligentiam custodum defendantur a plagis, possunt non vulnerari; quod si non custodiantur, possunt etiam vulnerari. Plurimum ergo distat inter ea quae a possibili veniunt, et ea quae a necessario; quae nisi custodiatur distinctio, in innumeros itur errores. Quod ut comparatione clarescat: lapsi sunt quidam medicinae oppugnatores, argumentati hanc artem nihil habere utilitatis; disputantque hoc modo: Moriturisne medicina subvenit, an victuris? Si morituris, nihil promovet; si victuris, frustra gestit. Qui enim morituri erant, hac quoque laborante, morientur; qui victuri, sine quoque huius beneficio salvi esse potuerunt. Quam nempe concinna, quam urbana conclusio! Sed dissolvitur a propugnatoribus medicinae hoc modo: Haec ars, inquiunt, prodest nec victuris, nec morituris dumtaxat a necessario, sed a possibili id utrumque passuris; non ergo adiuvat medicina eum qui sine dubio moriturus est, quoniam facere immortalem non potest; sed neque ei subvenit, qui sine dubio futurus incolumis est; verum illi, qui si non curetur, periclitari potest; si curetur, liberari potest; sicut ergo nec victuro nec morituro a necessarii conditione subvenire, ita et morituro et victuro, sed a possibili, ars potest erudita prodesse. Illi ergo priores medicantum studiis obloquentes, propositionem a possibili inchoantem, necessarii fine clauserunt; quod disputationis genus in innumera extenditur. Verbi gratia, prohibet lex homicidium fieri, prohibet etiam negligentiae per quam in pericula ruitur occasionem dari, ut in tauro cornupeta [n85] , atque in domorum coronis [n86] . At potest dici: Victuro subvenit ista diligentia, an morituro? Si morituro, nihil promovet; si victuro, ex abundanti consulit; si utrumque hoc contrarium, et per impedimenta et sine impedimentis necessario consequentur. At hoc falsum est: optimo enim mortalibus iure consulitur, ut quod poterant pati sine diligentia, diligentiae opibus evadant. Aliud ergo est a possibili, aliud a necessario. Ostendamus, iam quid his anteloquiis adiuvemur. Fecit Deus hominem liberi arbitrii, naturae bonae; sed quae capax esset virtutum, quas sibi ex se mancipato animo comparasset; quod liberum arbitrium aliter constare non poterat, quam ut haberet etiam peccandi possibilitatem. Libertatem ergo a necessario habet, voluntatem a possibili. Non potest non esse liber; sed in neutram voluntatem cogi potest, factusque rei necessariae possibilis effectus. In possibili ergo peccari potest, in necessario non potest; quia necessario non actor, sed auctor ipse censetur; atque hoc quod potest homo ex integro Dei est, a possibili autem ipse actor expenditur.
pass_a_gloss: But those who feel in process do not always take from the necessary, but many from the possible. This it is allowed to see in all bodies, but a longer disputation is born; nevertheless let us give a few examples. It is the nature of bodies that they grow together by joining, are loosed by division; they are therefore capable of a wound, who suffer destruction. That they can therefore be wounded, they have from the necessary; but that they are wounded, from the possible. Thus from the necessary is the nature of possibility, although the effect of possibility is not necessary. For example, a horse, an ox, and similar living beings have a woundable nature, and therefore things capable of inconvenience are from the necessary; but that they are wounded is not always necessary. For if they are defended from blows by the diligence of guardians, they can not be wounded; but if they are not guarded, they can even be wounded. There is therefore a very great distance between those things which come from the possible and those which from the necessary; which distinction unless it is kept, one goes into countless errors. That it may shine by a comparison: certain opponents of medicine have fallen, having argued that this art has nothing of utility; and they dispute in this manner: Does medicine help those about to die, or those about to live? If those about to die, it promotes nothing; if those about to live, it exults in vain. For those who were about to die, this also laboring, will die; those about to live could have been safe even without this benefit. How neat indeed, how urban a conclusion! But it is dissolved by the champions of medicine in this manner: This art, they say, profits neither those about to live, nor those about to die at least from the necessary, but those about to suffer each from the possible; medicine therefore does not help him who is without doubt about to die, because it cannot make him immortal; but neither does it help him who is without doubt about to be unharmed; but that one, who if he is not cured can be endangered; if he is cured, can be freed; as therefore it cannot help either one about to live or one about to die from the condition of the necessary, so an erudite art can profit both one about to die and one about to live, but from the possible. Those earlier ones therefore contradicting the studies of physicians began a proposition from the possible, they closed it with the end of the necessary; which kind of disputation is extended into countless things. For example, the law forbids homicide to be done, it also forbids an occasion of negligence through which one rushes into dangers to be given, as in a goring bull, and in the crowns of houses. But it can be said: Does that diligence help one about to live, or one about to die? If one about to die, it promotes nothing; if one about to live, it consults from abundance; if each this contrary, they will necessarily follow both through impediments and without impediments. But this is false: for it is consulted for mortals by the best right, that what they could suffer without diligence they may escape by the resources of diligence. One thing therefore is from the possible, another from the necessary. Let us show now by what we are helped by these prefaces. God made the human of free decision, of a good nature; but which would be capable of virtues, which he would have furnished for himself from a mind enslaved to himself; which free decision could not otherwise stand, than that he would have even a possibility of sinning. He has therefore freedom from the necessary, will from the possible. He cannot not be free; but he can be compelled toward neither will, and a possible effect of a necessary thing has been made. In the possible therefore one can sin, in the necessary one cannot; because in the necessary not the actor, but the author himself is judged; and this which the human can from the intact is God's, but from the possible the actor himself is weighed.

pass_b_english: But what they experience as they go on does not always come from necessity: much comes from possibility. This can be seen in every body, though it would require a longer discussion. Let us give a few examples. Bodies by nature grow together through combination and break apart through division. Those subject to destruction are therefore capable of injury. Their capacity to be wounded comes from necessity; their actually being wounded comes from possibility. Thus the nature of a possibility comes from necessity, although the realization of that possibility is not necessary. For example, a horse, an ox, and similar living creatures have a vulnerable nature, and necessarily possess the capacity for harm. Yet it is not always necessary that they be wounded. If their keepers’ care protects them from blows, they can remain unwounded; if they are not guarded, they can also be wounded. There is therefore a great difference between what arises from possibility and what arises from necessity. Unless this distinction is preserved, countless errors follow.

To make this clear by comparison: some opponents of medicine went astray, arguing that this art has no usefulness. They argue as follows: ‘Does medicine help those who will die or those who will live? If those who will die, it accomplishes nothing; if those who will live, its effort is pointless. Those who were going to die will die despite its labor; those who were going to live could have remained safe without its benefit.’ What a neat and polished conclusion! But medicine’s defenders dissolve it as follows: ‘This art helps neither those who will live nor those who will die by necessity, but those for whom either outcome is possible. Medicine does not help someone who will undoubtedly die, because it cannot make him immortal. Nor does it assist someone who will undoubtedly remain unharmed. It assists someone who can be in danger if untreated, but can be rescued if treated.’ Thus, just as the trained art cannot help someone destined to live or die by necessity, it can help those who may live or die as a matter of possibility. Those earlier critics of medical effort therefore closed with necessity an argument begun from possibility. This form of argument extends to countless matters.

For example, the law forbids homicide. It also forbids providing an occasion of negligence through which people fall into danger, as with a goring bull (Exodus 21:28–32) and the parapets of houses (Deuteronomy 22:8). Someone can say: ‘Does this care help a person who will live or one who will die? If one who will die, it accomplishes nothing; if one who will live, it takes needless precautions’—if these opposite outcomes necessarily follow whether obstacles are present or not. But that is false. Mortals are most rightly protected so that, through the resources of care, they escape what they could have suffered without care. What comes from possibility is therefore one thing; what comes from necessity is another.

Let us now show how these preliminaries help us. God made a human being with free will and a good nature, but one capable of virtues he could acquire for himself through a mind possessing its own freedom. This free will could not stand otherwise than by possessing also the possibility of sinning. A person therefore possesses freedom necessarily, while a particular act of will arises as a possibility. He cannot fail to be free, but cannot be compelled toward either will. A possible effect is thus produced by something necessary. In the possible sphere one can sin; in the necessary sphere one cannot. In the necessary sphere, the one assessed is not the actor but the creator himself: whatever the human being is capable of comes wholly from God. In the possible sphere, however, the actor himself is weighed.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
